17370:
A wedge is an object that is thick and wide at one end, and narrows down to a thin edge or point at the other end. If you look at it from the side, it looks like a triangle. That shape — wide on one side, thin on the other — is the defining characteristic of anything called a wedge.

Think of a doorstop. It's thick on one end and thin on the other. You slide the thin end under the door, and the thicker part holds the door open. That's a wedge.
The Wedge as a Tool or Simple Machine

The wedge is one of humanity's oldest and most fundamental tools. The idea is simple: you push force into the thick end, and the wedge converts that force sideways — pushing things apart, or holding things in place.

  • An axe head is a wedge. When you swing an axe into a log, the wedge shape forces the wood to split apart on both sides.
  • A knife blade is a wedge. The blade is thin at the cutting edge and wider as it rises — that's what allows it to slice through things.
  • A chisel is a wedge. It's hammered in to split or carve material.
  • A doorstop is a wedge used not to split, but to hold — the door presses against the sloped surface, and friction keeps it in place.

The key principle: the wedge transforms a pushing force into a splitting or holding force directed to the sides.
A Wedge as a Shape or Piece of Something

Because of its triangular shape, the word "wedge" is also used for any triangular or roughly triangular piece of something — especially food.

  • A wedge of cheese — a triangular slice cut from a round wheel of cheese.
  • A wedge of lemon — a small triangular piece cut from a lemon, used to squeeze juice onto food.
  • A wedge of cake — a triangular slice cut from a round cake.
  • A wedge salad — a quarter of a head of iceberg lettuce, served as a salad. It's called that because the lettuce is cut into a wedge shape.

So when you say "give me a wedge of that," you're asking for a triangular slice or chunk.

A wedge (also called a wedge heel or wedge shoe) is a type of shoe or sandal where the heel is a solid, continuous block that runs from the back of the shoe all the way under the middle of the foot. Unlike a stiletto or regular high heel — which has a thin, separate raised heel — the wedge heel is one solid piece forming a slope from the toe to the back.

The shape, again, follows the same principle: thin at the front, thicker toward the back, like a wedge lying on its side.

In golf, a wedge is a specific type of club. It has a steeply angled face, which means when you hit the ball, it launches high into the air and doesn't travel very far horizontally. Golfers use wedges for short-distance shots, especially to get out of sand or to land the ball precisely near the hole. Common types include the sand wedge, pitching wedge, and lob wedge.
Wedge in Military and Strategic Formations

A wedge formation is when soldiers, vehicles, or players in a sport arrange themselves in a triangular or V-shape, with one person or unit at the tip and the rest spreading out behind. The idea is that the pointed tip can break through enemy lines or defenses, while the broader rear provides support. Think of a flock of birds flying in a V — same concept.

This is one of the most important and commonly used meanings. A wedge can represent something that causes separation or division between people, groups, or relationships.

When you say someone "drove a wedge" between two friends, it means they caused conflict or mistrust — splitting the friendship apart, just like a physical wedge splits wood.

  • "His lies drove a wedge between the two brothers."
  • "The disagreement over money became a wedge in their marriage."

A wedge issue in politics is a controversial topic that divides people — politicians sometimes deliberately bring it up to split the opposing side or unite their own supporters.

In weather science, a wedge refers to a zone or mass of air (usually high pressure) that is thick in one area and tapers as it extends outward — matching the shape of a wedge. You might hear of a "high-pressure wedge" pushing cold or warm air into a region.

Every use of the word "wedge" comes back to the same central image: something tapered — wide and thick on one end, thin on the other. Whether it's a tool that splits wood, a slice of cheese, a type of shoe, a golf club, or a metaphor for division — the concept of a tapering shape, and the function of pushing things apart or fitting tightly into a gap, runs through all of them.

If you remember one thing: a wedge is thick at one end, thin at the other — and that shape lets it split, hold, fit, or divide.
17371:
Wee simply means very small or tiny. If something is wee, it is small in size — noticeably, often charmingly so.

"She carried a wee kitten in her pocket."
"He lives in a wee cottage at the edge of the forest."

That's the foundation. But the word carries a lot more than just size, so read on.

What makes "wee" special is its emotional tone. While "small" is a plain, neutral fact — like a measurement — "wee" is warm, soft, and affectionate. When someone calls something "wee," they often feel fond of it, or they want you to find it endearing or charming.

Compare:

  • "It's a small dog." → neutral, descriptive
  • "It's a wee dog." → gentle, affectionate, almost like a smile in a word

This is why parents call babies "a wee one," and why someone might describe a child as "a wee lad" or "a wee girl" with warmth. The smallness isn't just physical — it feels precious.

"Wee" can also describe degree — meaning a little or slightly — not just physical size. In this use, it usually appears in the phrase "a wee bit."

"I'm a wee bit nervous about the exam." → slightly nervous
"Could you speak a wee bit louder?" → just a little louder
"This soup is a wee bit too salty." → mildly too salty

Here, "wee" isn't describing the size of an object — it's softening how much of a quality something has. It makes the statement gentler and less absolute.

There is one very common, fixed expression you must know: "the wee hours" (sometimes "the wee small hours"). This refers to the very early hours of the morning — roughly 1 AM, 2 AM, 3 AM — the quiet, still part of the night when almost everyone is asleep.

"They talked until the wee hours of the morning."
"She was still working at her desk in the wee hours."

Why "wee"? Because these hours feel tiny — a small sliver of time at the edge of night and day, easy to overlook on a clock. The phrase has an atmospheric, almost poetic quality to it. It's widely used in both writing and conversation.

You will hear "wee" most naturally and most often in Scottish English and Irish English. In Scotland especially, "wee" is an everyday, all-purpose word for small — used constantly, without any special effort. A Scottish person might say "just a wee minute" the way others say "just a second."

In British English more broadly, it is understood and used, but it has a slightly informal or affectionate quality — it's not the default word for small the way it is in Scotland.

In American English, it is understood but less commonly used in everyday speech. When Americans use it, it often sounds deliberately playful, literary, or old-fashioned.

So: if you encounter "wee" in literature, film, or conversation, it most likely signals a Scottish or Irish speaker, or a writer deliberately choosing a warm, slightly old-world tone.

FeelWordExample

Here's how "wee" sits among similar words:

Small — neutral and factual. No emotion, no special tone. The default word.

Little — similar to "wee" in that it can be affectionate ("my little sister"), but far more common and versatile in everyday English.

Tiny — emphasises extreme smallness, almost surprising smallness. Stronger than "small." No particular warmth — just emphasis.

Wee — small, but with softness and fondness attached. Often used for living things or things you feel something for. Carries a cultural flavor (Scottish/Irish) that the others don't.

So "wee" isn't just a synonym for "small" — it comes wrapped in a particular emotional quality and regional identity.
Quick Summary of All Its Uses

1. Physically small: "a wee bird," "a wee room," "a wee child"
  2. A little bit (degree): "a wee bit tired," "a wee bit strange"
  3. Early hours: "the wee hours of the morning"
  4. Affectionate / endearing tone: applies to most uses above — it makes whatever it describes feel gentle and dear
One Thing to Keep in Mind

Because "wee" carries a regional and informal character, it generally doesn't suit formal writing — a business report, an academic essay, a legal document. In those contexts, "small" or "minor" or "slight" would be appropriate. But in storytelling, casual speech, poetry, or any context with a warm and personal tone, "wee" fits beautifully.

That's everything you need to know about "wee" as an adjective — its meaning, its feeling, how it's used, where it comes from, and how it differs from words like it.
17372:
As a noun, wee means urine — the liquid your body produces and releases when you go to the bathroom. It also refers to the act of urinating — the event of going to the bathroom to release that liquid.

Both meanings are closely linked, so the word covers both: the substance and the action.
Register: Where Does This Word Belong?

Wee is an informal, everyday word. It is not rude or vulgar — it sits comfortably in polite, casual conversation. You would not use it in a medical report (where the correct word is urine), but you would naturally use it when talking to friends, family, or children.

It is especially common in British, Irish, Scottish, and Australian English. You will hear it constantly in the UK and Ireland in particular. While speakers in North America more commonly use the word pee, wee is widely understood everywhere in the English-speaking world.
Two Faces of the Same Word

The word "wee" as a noun appears in two slightly different but connected ways:

1. Wee as the substance (urine itself)

Here, wee refers to the liquid — what comes out of the body.

"There is wee on the bathroom floor."
"The dog left wee on the carpet."
"The doctor needs a sample of your wee."

In this use, wee behaves like an uncountable noun — you don't say "a wee" or "two wees." You just say "wee," the same way you say "water" or "milk."

2. Wee as the act (a single instance of urinating)

Here, wee refers to one occasion of going to the bathroom to urinate — the event itself, not the liquid.

"I need a wee." (I need to go urinate.)
"She did a wee before the journey."
"He went for a wee."
"The baby had a wee on the floor."

In this use, wee is a countable noun — you say "a wee," "one wee," "two wees."

Here are the most natural ways this noun appears in everyday speech:

  • "need a wee" — to feel the urge to urinate

    "Can we stop soon? I really need a wee."

  • "have a wee" — to urinate (the event)

    "Go have a wee before we leave the house."

  • "do a wee" — same as "have a wee," just phrased differently

    "The little boy did a wee in his pants."

  • "go for a wee" — to go somewhere (like a toilet) to urinate

    "I'll be back in a moment — I'm just going for a wee."

  • "a quick wee" — a brief trip to urinate

    "Just give me two minutes; I need a quick wee."

Adults talking to children: Parents and caregivers use wee all the time with young children because it feels gentle and non-embarrassing.

"Do you need a wee? Tell me before it's too late."

Children themselves: Children in British and Irish English grow up using this word naturally.

Adults talking to other adults: Perfectly normal among friends and family in British, Irish, and Australian contexts.

"I drank so much tea that I was doing a wee every hour."

It is less formal than saying "I need to use the restroom" or "I need to urinate," but it is more polite than crude slang. Think of it as the comfortable, everyday middle ground.

Urine is the formal, clinical word used in medicine and science. Wee and pee are the informal equivalents — both mean the same thing. The main difference between them is geography: wee is the more natural choice in British, Irish, Scottish, and Australian English, while pee is more common in American English. Both are understood everywhere.

Wee also exists as an adjective meaning small or tiny — especially in Scottish English ("a wee bit," "a wee child"). That is a completely separate meaning. When someone says "I need a wee", the word wee is a noun meaning urination — not an adjective meaning tiny.

The context always makes the meaning clear.

As a noun, wee means urine (the liquid itself) or an act of urinating (the event of going to the toilet). It is a friendly, informal, non-vulgar word used widely in British, Irish, and Australian English. You use it when talking about the need to urinate, the act of urinating, or the liquid produced. It is the casual, everyday alternative to the formal word urine, and closely equivalent to pee in meaning.
17373:
To weep means to cry — to shed tears because of a strong emotion. That emotion is almost always sadness, grief, or sorrow, though sometimes it can be an overwhelming positive feeling like joy or relief.

She wept when she heard that her father had passed away.
He wept with joy when his daughter was born healthy.

Both words mean shedding tears, but they are not exactly the same in feel and usage.

"Cry" is a broad, everyday word. You can cry when you stub your toe, when you're frustrated, when you watch a sad movie, or when you're a baby wanting milk. It covers all kinds of crying.

"Weep" is deeper and more serious. It suggests a quieter, more profound kind of crying — often flowing tears of genuine grief or overwhelming emotion, rather than a sudden outburst. It carries a sense of dignity and depth. When someone weeps, it usually means they are truly, deeply moved. Because of this, "weep" is more formal and literary — you'll find it more often in books, poetry, religious texts, news writing about tragedies, and formal speech than in casual everyday conversation.

Think of it this way: a child cries when they fall. A mother weeps at her child's grave. Both involve tears, but the weight is very different.

"Weep" does not follow the regular pattern (weep → weeped). It is an irregular verb.

  • Base form: weep
  • Past tense: wept
  • Past participle: wept
  • Present participle: weeping
  • Third person singular (present): weeps

She weeps every time she thinks about it. (present)
She wept all night. (past)
She has wept before, but never like this. (past participle)
She was weeping silently in the corner. (continuous)

The past tense "wept" is especially important to remember, since it's completely different from "weep."

Knowing which prepositions follow "weep" helps you use it naturally:

  • weep for — to cry on behalf of someone or something, out of sympathy or loss
    The nation wept for the victims of the disaster.
  • weep over — to cry about something, often something that has already happened
    She wept over her mistakes.
  • weep with — to cry because of an emotion that fills you completely
    They wept with relief when the hostages were freed.
    He wept with grief at the funeral.
  • weep at — to cry in response to something specific
    Everyone wept at the news.
  • weep about — to cry concerning something (similar to "weep over," slightly more conversational)
    There's nothing to weep about now — it's over.

These phrases sound natural and are frequently used with "weep":

  • weep bitterly — to cry with deep pain and resentment
    She wept bitterly after the betrayal.
  • weep openly / weep openly — to cry without hiding it, in front of others
    He wept openly at the ceremony, and no one judged him.
  • weep silently — to cry without making sound
    She sat weeping silently by the window.
  • weep tears of joy — to cry because of extreme happiness
    The grandmother wept tears of joy at her granddaughter's wedding.
  • weep in someone's arms — to cry while being held by someone
    She wept in her mother's arms for hours.
A wider, figurative meaning — when things (not people) "weep"

"Weep" is also used to describe something that slowly drips or oozes liquid — the idea being that it looks as though it is "crying."

1. Wounds or sores:
When a wound is infected or not healing properly, it can ooze fluid. We say the wound is weeping.

The cut on his leg was weeping, so the doctor cleaned and bandaged it.
A weeping wound needs immediate medical attention.

2. Walls or surfaces:
When moisture seeps through walls or surfaces, we sometimes say the wall is weeping.

After the heavy rains, the basement walls were weeping with moisture.

3. Plants — the "weeping willow":
You may have heard of a weeping willow — it's a type of tree whose long, thin branches hang down low toward the ground, as if drooping with sadness, like someone bent over crying. This is where the name comes from. The drooping shape is compared to the posture of weeping.

This figurative use is easy to remember: anything that slowly drips, oozes, or droops "as if crying" can be described as weeping.

Use weep when:

  • The emotion is deep, serious, and genuine — especially grief, sorrow, or overwhelming joy
  • You're writing something formal, literary, or poetic
  • You want to convey more weight and dignity than "cry" would give
  • You're describing something (like a wound) that is slowly oozing fluid

Stick to cry when:

  • Speaking casually in conversation
  • The crying is ordinary or minor (a child crying, crying from frustration, crying at a movie)
  • You want a neutral, simple word
A few final example sentences to bring it all together

Thousands wept in the streets after the king's death.
She wept for her lost childhood, for the years she could never get back.
He had not wept in twenty years, but that day, he wept.
The doctor noted that the patient's wound was weeping and prescribed antibiotics.
Under the weeping willow, she sat alone and wept.
They wept with relief — the surgery had been a success.
"Weep not," he said gently, taking her hands in his.

That is everything there is to know about weep as a verb — its core meaning, how it differs from "cry," its irregular forms, the prepositions and phrases it goes with, its figurative uses, and when to reach for it. You now have a complete picture of this word.
17374: Weigh means to find out how heavy something is, or to be a certain heaviness. But the word has grown far beyond that — it is used in everyday physical situations, in thinking and decision-making, and in describing emotional burden. All its meanings connect back to the same central image: heaviness.
Meaning 1 — To Measure How Heavy Something Is

This is the most basic, literal meaning: to use a scale or balance to find out the weight of something.

You are the one doing the action — you are actively measuring.

Examples:

  • The shopkeeper weighed the mangoes before putting them in the bag.
  • She weighed her luggage to make sure it was under the airline limit.
  • The doctor weighed the newborn baby right after birth.
  • The jeweller weighed the gold ring carefully.
Meaning 2 — To Have a Certain Weight

Here, something is not being measured by someone — instead, the subject itself has that weight. The focus is on what the thing's weight is.

Examples:

  • This suitcase weighs 20 kilograms.
  • The elephant weighs more than 4,000 kilograms.
  • How much do you weigh?
  • The parcel weighed almost nothing — it was just paper inside.

Notice the difference from Meaning 1: in Meaning 1, someone is doing the weighing. In Meaning 2, the subject simply is a certain weight — no action is happening, only a state of being.
Meaning 3 — To Think Carefully and Compare (The Most Important Figurative Meaning)

This is where weigh becomes truly powerful in English. When you weigh ideas, choices, or options, you are mentally placing them on an imaginary scale — examining each side, comparing them, and thinking seriously before you decide.

Just as a physical scale reveals which side is heavier, your mind is trying to find out which option, argument, or fact is "heavier" — that is, more important, more convincing, or more valuable.

Examples:

  • Before accepting the job offer, he weighed all the pros and cons.
  • The judge must weigh the evidence on both sides before giving a verdict.
  • She weighed her words carefully before she spoke, so as not to offend anyone.
  • You should weigh the risks before investing your savings.
  • The committee will weigh the benefits of the new policy against its costs.

The phrase "weigh your words" deserves special attention. It means to think very carefully about exactly what you say — to consider the effect each word might have — before speaking or writing. It suggests precision and deliberateness.
Meaning 4 — To Press Down On Someone (As a Burden)

Here, weigh describes how something heavy — not physically, but emotionally or mentally — presses down on a person. It is used to show that something is troubling, burdening, or oppressing someone.

The image is clear: just as a heavy object presses down on a scale, worry, guilt, or sadness presses down on a person's mind or spirit.

Examples:

  • The guilt of his mistake weighed on him for years.
  • The responsibility of leading the entire team weighed heavily on her.
  • Bad news always weighs on his mind.
  • The secret she was hiding weighed on her conscience.
Meaning 5 — To Matter / To Have Influence in a Decision

When something weighs in a decision or argument, it means it has importance, influence, or impact. It "pulls" the decision in one direction, just as weight on a scale pulls the pan down.

Examples:

  • Her experience in the field weighed heavily in the committee's decision to hire her.
  • His past criminal record weighed against him at the trial.
  • The new evidence weighed in favour of the accused.
  • Price is not the only thing that weighs in a purchasing decision — quality matters too.
Common Phrasal Verbs and Set Expressions

Phrasal verbs are combinations of weigh + another word that together create a specific meaning.

Weigh on / Weigh upon

Meaning: To trouble, worry, or oppress someone; to be a source of continuous mental or emotional pressure.

  • The unsolved problem weighed on his mind all night.
  • The thought of leaving her family behind weighed upon her deeply.

Weigh down

Meaning: (1) To make something physically heavy, so it sinks, bends, or is pulled toward the ground. (2) To burden someone emotionally, making them feel sad, tired, or oppressed.

  • The fruit had grown so large that it weighed down the branches of the tree.
  • She was weighed down by grief after losing her friend.
  • Too many responsibilities can weigh you down and affect your health.

Weigh up

Meaning: To carefully consider and evaluate something — especially options, risks, or situations — before making a decision. Very commonly used in British English.

  • I need some time to weigh up my options before I give you an answer.
  • She weighed up the situation and decided it was too risky.
  • Before signing the contract, make sure you weigh up all the terms.

Weigh against

Meaning: To consider one thing in comparison with something else, especially to judge whether the advantages are greater than the disadvantages, or vice versa.

  • The company weighed the high cost of the project against its long-term benefits.
  • You must weigh the pleasure of eating junk food against its effect on your health.
  • The benefits of the new law were carefully weighed against its possible negative effects.

Weigh in

Meaning 1 (literal): In sports like boxing, wrestling, or horse racing, to be officially weighed before a competition.

  • The boxer weighed in at 72 kilograms before the championship fight.

Meaning 2 (figurative): To join a conversation, debate, or discussion by offering your opinion or contribution — especially when what you say is significant.

  • Several experts weighed in on the debate about climate change.
  • The Prime Minister finally weighed in with his view on the economic crisis.
  • After everyone had spoken, she weighed in with a point nobody had considered.

Weigh out

Meaning: To measure a specific quantity of something by weight — usually in precise, careful amounts.

  • The pharmacist weighed out the exact dose of medicine.
  • The baker weighed out 200 grams of flour for the recipe.

Weigh anchor

Meaning: A nautical (sailing) expression meaning to lift the anchor from the seabed so that a ship can begin to move and sail away. "Weighing" the anchor here means lifting it, as if measuring its heaviness as you pull it up.

  • At dawn, the captain gave the order to weigh anchor and set sail.
Putting It All Together: The Central Image

Every meaning of weigh connects back to one idea — heaviness and balance.

  • When you weigh an object, you find out its heaviness.
  • When something weighs 10 kilos, that is its heaviness.
  • When you weigh a decision, you are testing the heaviness of each option in your mind.
  • When something weighs on you, it sits heavy on your mind.
  • When something weighs in favour of a choice, it adds heaviness — importance — to that side of the argument.

If you always come back to the image of a scale with two pans, and something pressing down with its weight, you will never be confused by this word.
17375: Weight refers to how heavy something is, or the force that pulls something downward. Almost every meaning of "weight" branches out from this central idea of heaviness and the effect it has — whether on a physical object, a decision, a person's mind, or a system.
1. How heavy something is (the most common, everyday meaning)

This is what most people mean when they use the word "weight" in daily life. It's the measure of how much an object presses down when placed on a surface.

"The weight of the box is 10 kilograms."
"She gained weight after the holidays."
"The bridge can hold a maximum weight of five tonnes."

Weight is usually measured in kilograms (kg), pounds (lbs), grams (g), tonnes, etc. When you step on a scale, what it shows is your weight.
2. The force of gravity pulling something down (the scientific meaning)

In science — specifically physics — "weight" has a precise meaning that is slightly different from everyday usage.

Weight is a force. It is the gravitational pull that the Earth (or any planet) exerts on an object. The more mass an object has, and the stronger the gravity, the greater its weight.

This is why astronauts on the Moon weigh much less than they do on Earth — the Moon's gravity is weaker. Their mass stays the same, but their weight changes.

In physics, weight is measured in Newtons (N), not kilograms.

"The weight of a 10 kg object on Earth is approximately 98 Newtons."

Weight vs. Mass — an important distinction:

  • Mass is the amount of matter in an object. It never changes, no matter where you are in the universe.
  • Weight is the force of gravity on that mass. It changes depending on where you are.

In everyday conversation, people use "weight" and "mass" interchangeably (saying "I weigh 60 kg"), but strictly speaking, kilograms measure mass, not weight. For everyday purposes, this confusion is harmless, but it's good to know the difference.
3. A heavy object (a physical "weight")

The word "weight" is also used to refer to a physical object that is heavy by design — made to be heavy for a specific purpose.

Gym weights / dumbbells: The heavy metal pieces you lift in a gym.

"He picked up a 10 kg weight and started curling."

Weights on a scale: Small, precisely measured pieces of metal placed on a balance scale to measure how heavy something else is.

"The jeweller used tiny weights to measure the gold."

A paperweight: A small, heavy object placed on papers to stop them from blowing away.

"She kept a glass paperweight on her desk."

A counterweight: A weight placed on one side of a machine or system to balance the other side.

"The crane uses a large counterweight to stay balanced."
4. Importance, influence, or significance

This is one of the most common figurative (non-physical) uses of the word. When something "carries weight," it means it matters, it has power, it has influence on how people think or decide.

"His recommendation carries a lot of weight — people trust his opinion."
"The professor's words had great weight with the students."
"Her evidence gave more weight to the argument."
"The committee gave little weight to his concerns."

Here, "weight" is not about heaviness at all — it's about how seriously something is taken. Just like a heavier object is harder to ignore or move, an important opinion or piece of evidence is harder to dismiss.
5. A burden — something heavy to carry, physically or emotionally

Weight is also used to describe anything that feels like a heavy burden — something that presses down on you, makes life harder, or causes suffering.

Physical burden:

"The weight of the rucksack made hiking exhausting."

Emotional or mental burden:

"She felt the weight of grief after losing her father."
"The weight of responsibility rested on his shoulders."
"He carried the weight of his past mistakes everywhere he went."

The image here is intuitive: just as a heavy physical load is tiring and difficult to bear, so too is an emotional or moral load. We naturally describe difficult feelings and responsibilities using the language of heaviness.
6. The weight of a decision or situation

Closely related to the idea of burden and importance, "weight" can refer to the seriousness or gravity of a situation.

"He paused, feeling the full weight of what he was about to do."
"The judge understood the weight of her decision."
"The weight of the moment was not lost on anyone in the room."

This sense captures how certain moments, choices, or situations feel "heavy" — they demand attention, care, and seriousness.
7. Weight in statistics and data

In mathematics and statistics, a weight is a number assigned to a data point to show how much importance or influence it should have in a calculation.

For example, imagine a student's final grade is calculated like this: exams count more than homework. So exams are given a higher "weight." This is called weighting data.

"Each answer in the survey was given a different weight based on how reliable the source was."
"The weighted average gave more weight to recent data."

The logic is the same as in everyday life: something with more "weight" has more pull, more influence on the final result.
8. Weight in typography and design

In the world of fonts and graphic design, "weight" refers to how thick or thin the strokes of letters are.

"This heading uses a bold weight font."
"The designer chose a light weight for the body text."

You may have seen font options like: Thin, Light, Regular, Medium, Bold, Heavy, Black. These are all different "weights" of the same font. A heavier weight means thicker, bolder letters.
9. Weight in fabric and materials

In textiles and manufacturing, "weight" describes how thick, dense, or heavy a material is per unit of area.

"This winter coat is made from a heavy-weight wool."
"The light-weight cotton is perfect for summer."
"The fabric weight is 200 grams per square metre."

A heavy-weight fabric is thick, warm, and durable. A light-weight fabric is thin, breathable, and easy to move in.
Common phrases and expressions using "weight"

These phrases come up often in English and are worth knowing:

"To pull your weight" — to do your fair share of work.

"Everyone on the team needs to pull their weight."

"To throw your weight around" — to use your power or authority in an aggressive, bossy way.

"The new manager kept throwing his weight around, which upset the staff."

"To throw your weight behind something" — to actively support something with all your influence.

"The senator threw her weight behind the new bill."

"Dead weight" — something (or someone) that is a burden and contributes nothing useful.

"That old machine is just dead weight — it should be thrown away."

"To carry weight" — to be important or credible.

"His long experience in the field carries weight."

"Worth its weight in gold" — extremely valuable.

"A good teacher is worth their weight in gold."

"The weight of the world on one's shoulders" — to feel as though you are responsible for everything and are under enormous pressure.

"After losing the company's biggest client, she felt the weight of the world on her shoulders."

"Under the weight of" — collapsing or struggling because of something heavy — literally or figuratively.

"The old shelf buckled under the weight of the books."
"He crumbled under the weight of expectations."
Putting it all together

The word "weight" is remarkably versatile, but it always comes back to one central idea: heaviness and the effect it has. Whether you are talking about how many kilograms something measures, the gravitational force pulling an object down, a metal disc used for lifting, the seriousness of a decision, the burden of grief, the influence of an opinion, or the thickness of a font — all of these are variations of the same human instinct to describe what is heavy, what presses down, and what demands to be taken seriously.

Understanding this single thread — heaviness as force, burden, and importance — will help you recognise and use "weight" correctly in almost any context you encounter it.
17376:
Think about what happens when you hold something physically heavy in your hands. It demands your attention. You can't ignore it. You feel its presence. You have to deal with it carefully.

The adjective weighty takes that same feeling — the feeling of heaviness — and applies it to things that are not always physical. Something weighty is something that carries real, serious significance or importance, something you cannot brush aside lightly.

Weighty has a few related uses, and they all revolve around the idea of "heaviness" — either literal or metaphorical.

1. Physically Heavy (Literal Use)

In its most straightforward sense, weighty simply means heavy in physical weight.

"The workers struggled to lift the weighty stone blocks."

This use is not very common in everyday speech. Most people just say "heavy." But "weighty" still works here, and you will encounter it occasionally in writing.

2. Serious, Important, and Significant (Most Common Use)

This is by far the most frequent meaning. When something is called weighty, it means it is serious, significant, and deserving of careful thought and attention. It is the kind of thing you cannot handle carelessly or dismiss without consideration.

"The scientists gathered to discuss a weighty question: Is there life on other planets?"

"The president had to make a weighty decision that would affect millions of people."

"They spent hours debating weighty matters of law and justice."

Notice the pattern: weighty things are not trivial. They are not small talk or minor inconveniences. They carry real consequence — in life, in relationships, in society, in history. When you describe something as weighty, you are signalling to your listener: pay attention, this matters.

3. Difficult to Bear — A Burden

When you carry something heavy for a long time, it becomes exhausting. It weighs you down. In the same way, weighty can describe something that is burdensome — difficult to carry emotionally, morally, or mentally.

"She accepted the weighty responsibility of caring for her entire family."

"The guilt was weighty, pressing down on him with every passing day."

Here, "weighty" conveys not just importance, but also the strain and heaviness that comes with it. The thing is not just significant — it costs something.

4. Powerful and Convincing (For Arguments, Reasons, Evidence)

When used to describe an argument, reason, or piece of evidence, weighty means difficult to ignore or dismiss — convincing and forceful.

"She made a weighty argument that the policy needed to change."

"The defence lawyer presented weighty evidence in favour of his client."

A weighty argument is one that lands with force and carries real logical or moral power behind it. It is not easily brushed aside.

5. Influential and Authoritative (For People or Opinions)

Weighty can also describe a person, opinion, or voice that holds great authority, influence, or importance in a particular area.

"A weighty figure in the world of science, she had published over 200 papers."

"His weighty opinion swayed the entire committee."

When a person is "weighty," they are not just important in a vague sense — they carry clout. Their words and decisions have real impact.

Every meaning of weighty traces back to the same idea: something that has real substance and cannot be taken lightly.

UseWhat it means

Here is the thread in words: a heavy object demands your physical effort. A heavy topic demands your mental and emotional effort. A heavy responsibility demands your time and sacrifice. A heavy argument demands your serious consideration. A heavy person demands your respect and attention. That thread — you cannot take this lightly — runs through every use of weighty.

Weighty is a slightly formal word. You are more likely to read it in books, newspapers, and essays than to hear it in casual conversation. In everyday speech, people tend to say "serious," "important," or "big" instead. But in writing, weighty adds a layer of gravitas — a sense that something is not just important, but deeply important.

It also carries a neutral-to-slightly-solemn tone. You wouldn't use "weighty" to describe something exciting or joyful. Weighty things are serious things.
What Weighty Is Often Used With

To get a feel for the word, here are the kinds of nouns you will typically see it paired with:

  • Weighty matter / issue / subject / topic — something serious that requires careful thought
  • Weighty decision / choice — a decision with major consequences
  • Weighty responsibility / burden / obligation — something difficult and important to carry
  • Weighty argument / evidence / reason — something convincing and forceful
  • Weighty question / debate — a serious, significant discussion
  • Weighty figure / authority / voice — a person or entity of great influence

Weighty = heavy in importance, seriousness, or significance. It describes things that cannot be taken lightly — whether that is a physical object, a decision, a responsibility, an argument, or a person's influence. The word carries a formal, serious tone and is more common in writing than in casual speech. It always says: this has real substance; handle with care.
17377:
To weld means to permanently join two or more pieces of material — usually metal — by melting them at the point where they meet, so they fuse together and, upon cooling, become one solid piece.

That's the core idea.
What actually happens when you weld?

When a welder works, they apply an intense source of heat — often an electric arc, a flame, or a laser — directly to the spot where two pieces of metal touch or are placed edge-to-edge. The heat is so extreme that the metal at that spot literally melts into a small pool of liquid. The two separate molten edges flow into each other. Once the heat is removed, the pool cools down and solidifies. The result is no longer two pieces held together — it is now one continuous piece of metal. The join point is called a weld (the noun form).

Critically, this is not like gluing or screwing things together, where the materials stay separate and something external holds them. In welding, the materials themselves merge. This is why welded joints are extremely strong — often as strong as, or even stronger than, the original material around them.
Is a filler material always used?

Not always, but very often. Sometimes the two base pieces alone provide enough melted metal to fill the joint. But in many cases, a welder feeds in a filler material — a metal rod or wire — into the molten pool to reinforce and fill any gap. This filler is chosen to be compatible with (and usually the same type of metal as) the pieces being joined.

Metals are by far the most common — steel, iron, aluminum, stainless steel, copper, and many others. Welding is everywhere in construction, manufacturing, automotive work, shipbuilding, and plumbing.

Certain plastics (thermoplastics) can also be welded. The process is similar: you heat the plastic at the joint, it softens and flows together, and then it hardens into one piece upon cooling. This is used in making water pipes, car bumpers, and some packaging.

You cannot weld wood, glass (in the conventional sense), or most brittle materials, because they don't melt and flow the way metals and thermoplastics do.
How is welding different from similar processes?

It helps to contrast welding with related techniques people sometimes confuse it with:

  • Soldering and brazing also use heat to join metals, but the key difference is that in soldering/brazing, only the filler material melts — the base metals do not. This makes the bond weaker than a true weld, where the base metals themselves fuse.
  • Bolting or riveting joins pieces mechanically without any melting at all. The pieces stay separate; a fastener holds them. A welded joint has no such external fastener — the material itself is the bond.
The different ways welding is done

There isn't just one method of welding. The word covers a family of techniques that all achieve the same result — fusion of materials — but through different means:

  • Arc welding uses electricity to create a plasma arc between an electrode and the workpiece, generating intense heat. This is the most common form and is what most people picture when they think of welding — the bright sparks, the protective face shield.
  • MIG welding (Metal Inert Gas) is a type of arc welding where a wire electrode is fed automatically into the weld pool, and an inert gas shields the area from atmospheric contamination.
  • TIG welding (Tungsten Inert Gas) is a more precise, controlled version, where the welder holds a non-consumable tungsten electrode in one hand and a separate filler rod in the other. It's used for delicate, high-quality work.
  • Oxy-fuel welding uses a flame produced by burning a fuel gas (like acetylene) mixed with oxygen. It's older and slower but still used in certain applications.
  • Spot welding presses two metal sheets together and passes an electric current through the contact point, fusing them in a small "spot." You'll see this in car manufacturing.
  • Laser welding uses a focused laser beam for very precise, clean welds, common in electronics and medical equipment.

All of these are instances of the verb "to weld." The method changes; the concept doesn't.

Literal use:

  • "The workers welded the steel beams together to form the bridge's frame."
  • "She welded the cracked exhaust pipe back into one piece."
  • "The factory welded thousands of car bodies in a single day using robotic arms."
  • "He carefully welded the two aluminum plates along their seam."

Notice that you can weld things together, weld things to something, or simply weld things (and the context makes the joining clear).
The figurative meaning — and it's widely used

"To weld" is also used figuratively in everyday English to describe the act of uniting people, groups, or ideas into a single, inseparable whole. The logic is exactly the same as the literal sense: separate things are joined so tightly that they effectively become one.

  • "The long expedition had welded the team into a tight, unbreakable unit."
  • "Their shared suffering welded the two families together forever."
  • "A great leader can weld diverse people into a common cause."
  • "Hardship welded their friendship into something unshakeable."

When used figuratively, "weld" implies a bond that is deep, permanent, and not easily undone — not a casual or temporary connection. It's a stronger word than simply "unite" or "bring together." It suggests the kind of bond that forms under pressure or intensity, one where the original separateness is gone.
The strength and permanence — the soul of the word

What unifies both the literal and figurative use of "weld" is the idea of irreversible fusion. After welding, there is no easy way to get the original separate pieces back. You have created something new and unified from what was once multiple parts. This is the defining character of the word — not just joining, but fusing, melting into one, creating a bond at a fundamental level.

This is why "weld" is the right word when you want to emphasize not merely connection, but deep, lasting, structural unity.
17378:
Welfare means the condition of being well — well in every important sense of the word: healthy, safe, comfortable, happy, and free from suffering. It describes the overall quality of someone's life or existence.

Think of it as an umbrella word that covers all the things that make life good for a person (or an animal, or a group of people): their physical health, their mental peace, their financial security, their safety, and their general happiness. When all of these things are in a good state, we say their welfare is good. When they are suffering, struggling, or in danger, we say their welfare is at risk or in poor condition.

Welfare carries two related but distinct meanings, and both are very commonly used.

Meaning 1: General Wellbeing

This is the original and broader meaning. Here, welfare simply means the state of doing well — being okay in life. It's about health, safety, happiness, and comfort.

You'll often see this in sentences where someone is showing care or concern for another person or creature:

  • "The nurse checked on the patient's welfare every few hours." — She was checking whether the patient was okay, comfortable, and not in pain.
  • "The organization works for the welfare of homeless children." — It works to improve the lives and living conditions of homeless children.
  • "Parents are responsible for their child's welfare." — Parents must ensure their child is safe, healthy, fed, educated, and emotionally cared for.
  • "The soldiers' welfare was the general's top priority." — Their safety, health, and morale mattered most to him.

Notice that in all these examples, welfare is not about money specifically — it's about the totality of someone's condition in life.

Meaning 2: Government Financial Assistance

In everyday speech — especially in the United States — welfare is also used as a shorthand term for government programs that provide money, food, housing, or other support to people who are poor, unemployed, or otherwise unable to meet their basic needs on their own.

This meaning comes directly from the first one: the government steps in to support the welfare (wellbeing) of people who are struggling.

Examples:

  • "After losing her job, she applied for welfare." — She applied for government financial assistance to help cover her basic expenses.
  • "He grew up in a family that depended on welfare." — His family received government support because they couldn't afford essentials on their own.
  • "The debate about welfare reform has been going on for decades." — People disagree about how government assistance programs should be structured or changed.

This second meaning is more specific and context-bound. If you're reading or hearing about politics, poverty, or social policy — especially in an American context — this is usually what welfare refers to.

Understanding how welfare is used in combination with other words will help you recognize it and use it accurately.

"The welfare of [someone]" — This is the most natural phrase for Meaning 1. It simply means "how well [someone] is doing" or "the wellbeing of [someone]."

  • The welfare of the elderly.
  • The welfare of future generations.
  • The welfare of the nation.

"Animal welfare" — This refers to the humane treatment of animals — making sure they are not made to suffer unnecessarily. When you hear phrases like "animal welfare laws" or "animal welfare organizations," they are about protecting animals from cruelty and ensuring they have decent living conditions.

"Child welfare" — The safety, health, and proper care of children. Child welfare systems (run by governments) exist to protect children from abuse, neglect, or dangerous home situations.

"Social welfare" — An umbrella term for all the services and programs a government or society provides to support its people — healthcare, housing assistance, unemployment benefits, food support, and so on. It's the organized, large-scale effort by a society to protect the wellbeing of its members, especially the most vulnerable.

"Public welfare" — The general wellbeing of the community or the population as a whole. Laws, policies, and decisions are sometimes made "in the interest of public welfare," meaning for the good of everyone.

"Welfare state" — A type of government (or the system it runs) in which the state takes significant responsibility for the welfare of its citizens — through healthcare, education, unemployment support, pensions, and so on. Many European countries are considered welfare states.

"On welfare" — An informal phrase meaning receiving government financial assistance. "She was on welfare for two years before finding stable work."

"Welfare check" — This phrase has two completely different meanings depending on context:

  1. A visit (usually by police or social workers) to check that someone is physically safe and okay — often done when a person hasn't been heard from and someone is worried about them. "Her neighbor called for a welfare check when she didn't answer her door for several days."
  2. A payment check from a welfare (government assistance) program.
The Spectrum of Who or What Can Have Welfare

One useful thing to notice about welfare is how broadly it can be applied. It doesn't only apply to individual people. It can apply to:

  • Individuals: "His welfare improved after he received proper medical care."
  • Groups of people: "The welfare of migrant workers is often neglected."
  • Children specifically: "Child welfare laws protect minors from abuse."
  • Animals: "The farm was inspected for compliance with animal welfare standards."
  • Communities or nations: "Policies should prioritize the welfare of the most vulnerable communities."
  • Future generations: "We have a responsibility to protect the welfare of people who haven't been born yet."

This range makes welfare an extremely versatile word. The common thread across all uses is the same: it's about being in a good, healthy, secure, and dignified state.

You might wonder: what's the difference between welfare and wellbeing? They are very similar in meaning — almost interchangeable in many contexts — but there's a subtle difference in how they're used:

  • Wellbeing tends to feel more personal, internal, and holistic — it often includes emotional, psychological, and even spiritual dimensions. "Meditation improves your overall wellbeing."
  • Welfare is slightly more formal and is often used in institutional, legal, or social contexts — when talking about organizations, governments, policies, or duties of care. "The state has a duty to protect the welfare of its citizens."

Both mean roughly the same thing, but welfare sounds more official and is more likely to appear in laws, policy documents, or discussions about social responsibility.

Welfare is a word that sits at the intersection of ethics and care. Whenever it appears, it signals that someone is thinking about the responsibility one person, institution, or society has toward others — especially those who are vulnerable, dependent, or at risk. It carries a moral weight: to care about someone's welfare is to take their condition in life seriously and to do something about it when it's poor.

This is why it appears so often in discussions about children, animals, workers, the poor, and the elderly — groups that are often less able to protect or advocate for themselves.

Core meaningThe condition of being healthy, safe, comfortable, happy, and doing well in life
Social/political meaningGovernment programs that provide financial and material support to people in need
Who or what it applies toIndividuals, groups, animals, communities, nations
Key feeling the word carriesCare, responsibility, moral concern for the condition of others

Welfare, in short, means the condition of being well — safe, healthy, comfortable, and free from suffering. In a broader social sense, it refers to the overall quality of life for a person or group. In a political and policy sense, it refers specifically to government programs that support people who cannot meet their basic needs on their own. The word always carries an undertone of care and moral responsibility — it appears wherever someone is thinking about their duty to look after others.
17379:
Welkin means the sky — but not in the plain, everyday sense of "it's a cloudy sky today." It refers to the sky as a grand, sweeping, awe-inspiring dome that arches over the entire world. Think of it as the whole vast expanse of heaven spread above you, from one horizon to the other. Some descriptions also extend it slightly to mean the upper regions of the air, or the heavens in a broad, almost spiritual sense.

It is best to think of it not as the sky you glance at to check the weather, but the sky that makes you stop and feel small — that enormous blue or star-filled ceiling above all of humanity.
The tone and register of this word

This is not a word you will hear in everyday conversation. Welkin is archaic and poetic. It belongs to the language of old literature, classical poetry, and elevated or formal writing. If someone uses it in modern times, they are either:

  • Writing in a deliberately literary or old-fashioned style,
  • Trying to give their words a grand, majestic feeling, or
  • Using it humorously or ironically to sound overly dramatic.

You will encounter it most often when reading Shakespeare, old English poetry, historical novels, or works that imitate older styles of writing. It is never used in news articles, casual emails, or modern conversation. When you do come across it, it immediately signals that the writing is trying to feel elevated and timeless.
The most famous use: "Make the welkin ring"

There is a well-known phrase built around this word: "to make the welkin ring."

It means to produce a sound so enormously loud that it seems to fill the entire sky — as if the heavens themselves are vibrating. Imagine a massive crowd of thousands cheering wildly, or cannons firing, or bells clanging with such force that the noise rises all the way up and reverberates through the heavens. That is the idea.

This phrase is used both literally (a physically thunderous noise) and figuratively (celebrating with great, boisterous enthusiasm). You might read something like: "The crowd's roar made the welkin ring." It is a dramatic, colourful way of saying the noise was absolutely enormous.

Here are sentences that show the word used naturally, so you get a feel for it in context:

  • "The eagle soared through the welkin, disappearing into the blue vastness above."
  • "Stars began to emerge across the welkin as the last light of day faded."
  • "Their joyful shouts made the welkin ring with celebration."
  • "The poet gazed at the welkin and felt the full weight of his own smallness."

• It does not refer to weather specifically (rain, clouds, etc.) — those are things in the welkin, not the welkin itself.
  • It is not a scientific or technical term. Astronomers do not use it; poets do.
  • It does not mean outer space in the modern sense — it is the sky as seen and felt from the ground, the living canopy above us, not the cosmos beyond.
The key feeling to associate with this word

When you see welkin, think: the sky, described with grandeur and reverence. It is the kind of word that makes you look up. It transforms "the sky" from a background detail into something majestic and full of presence. Writers reach for it when ordinary words like "sky" or "heavens" feel too plain for what they are trying to convey.
Welkin = the sky or vault of heaven, used in a poetic or archaic register to give the sky a sense of grandeur and vastness.
